summary: A best current practice recommending that bidirectional RTP and RTCP sessions use one UDP port pair for both directions, commonly called symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP. Doing so makes such sessions easier to handle through NATs and firewalls.

plainLanguage.summary:
RTP and RTCP are two protocols that carry live media and its control messages over UDP. Neither one requires the sending and receiving sides to use the same port number, but a lot of equipment in the path assumes they do.

This RFC gives that arrangement a name, symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP, and recommends it for every two-way session. The device that receives media on port A sends its own media back out of port A. The arrangement is required behind some kinds of address translation and for media relays.

questions: rtp and rtcp port usage best practice
why does nat need symmetric rtp
symmetric rtp and rtcp port allocation
why symmetric rtp helps nat traversal
subtitle: One UDP port pair per session, used for both directions, so media survives NATs and firewalls.

tldr.problem: RTP and RTCP are not inherently bidirectional, so devices often picked a different UDP port for sending than for receiving. Many firewalls, NATs and RTP implementations expect the same port in both directions and simply fail otherwise.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP: a device that receives a media stream on UDP port A sends its own media for that stream from the same port A, and the same rule applies to the RTCP port.
tldr.outcome: Symmetric ports are REQUIRED behind NATs without an Application Layer Gateway and for media relays, and RECOMMENDED for all bidirectional RTP streams. The cost is that a single observed packet reveals the ports an attacker would need.

facts.value: Always, for bidirectional RTP media streams

today: RFC 4961 is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted, so symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP remain the recommended way to allocate ports for a bidirectional media session.

sections.title: Why Symmetric Ports Were Needed
sections.content:
TCP is inherently bidirectional. It transmits and receives on the same local port, so when a connection is established from host A with source port a, the remote host sends back to host A's source port a. UDP is not inherently bidirectional and does not require the same port for sending and receiving.

Some UDP applications use a single port for both directions, such as DNS. Some use different ports with explicit signalling, such as TFTP. Others, including RTP, do not specify the choice of transmit and receive ports at all.

Because RTP and RTCP are not inherently bidirectional, and UDP is not either, the usefulness of using the same UDP port for transmitting and receiving was generally ignored for RTP and RTCP. Many firewalls, Network Address Translators and RTP implementations expect symmetric RTP and do not work in the presence of asymmetric RTP. The term had never been defined, so this document defines it.

The ports themselves are chosen by the device that receives and transmits the media. For unicast flows, the receive port is communicated to the remote peer, for example in a Session Description Protocol carried in SIP, in the Session Announcement Protocol, or in Megaco. There is no correspondence between a local RTP or RTCP port and the remote one: device A might choose 1234 for both its transmit and receive port, and device B is not constrained to do the same, since that port may already be in use there.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP always uses one port for both directions. UDP does not, and RTP never said which ports to use. Firewalls and address translators often expect one port for both, so a session that uses different ports can fail.

sections.title: Requirement Words
sections.content: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Those capitalised words set how strongly each rule applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses the standard capitalised words for rules, so a reader can tell which parts are mandatory and which are advice.

sections.title: What Symmetric RTP and RTCP Mean
sections.content:
A device supports symmetric RTP if it selects, communicates and uses IP addresses and port numbers such that, when receiving a bidirectional RTP media stream on UDP port A and IP address a, it also transmits RTP media for that stream from the same source UDP port A and IP address a. It uses the same UDP port to transmit and receive one RTP stream. A device that does not support symmetric RTP would transmit RTP from a different port, or from a different IP address, than the port and address used to receive it.

A device supports symmetric RTCP if it selects, communicates and uses IP addresses and port numbers such that, when receiving RTCP packets for a media stream on UDP port B and IP address b, it also transmits RTCP packets for that stream from the same source UDP port B and IP address b. A device that does not support symmetric RTCP would transmit RTCP from a different port, or from a different IP address, than the one used to receive it.
sections.plainLanguage: Symmetric means the sending port and the receiving port are the same. If a device gets media on port A, it puts its own media back out of port A. The same rule applies separately to the control channel.

sections.title: When Symmetric Ports Are Required
sections.content:
There are two specific instances where symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP are REQUIRED.

The first is Network Address Translators that lack integrated Application Layer Gateway functionality. Such translators require that endpoints use symmetric UDP ports to establish bidirectional traffic, and the requirement exists for all of the translator behaviours described in RFC 4787.

The second is Session Border Controllers and other forms of RTP and RTCP relay. Media relays are necessary to establish bidirectional UDP communication across a translator that is address-dependent or address-and-port-dependent, but even with a media relay, symmetric UDP ports are still required to traverse such a translator.

There are other instances where symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP are helpful, but not required. A firewall that can expect symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP can use a more restrictive dynamic per-call port filter list than it could with asymmetric RTP and asymmetric RTCP. Symmetric ports can also ease debugging and troubleshooting. Other UDP-based protocols can benefit from common local transmit and receive ports. There are no known cases where symmetric RTP or symmetric RTCP are harmful.

For these reasons, it is RECOMMENDED that symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP always be used for bidirectional RTP media streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Symmetric ports are mandatory when the traffic crosses a NAT that has no helper for the application, and when a relay copies the media for it. Elsewhere they are recommended, because a firewall can then open fewer ports and troubleshooting is easier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an attacker learns the source and destination UDP ports of a symmetric RTP or symmetric RTCP flow, the attacker can send RTP or RTCP packets to that host. This differs from asymmetric RTP and asymmetric RTCP, where an attacker has to learn the UDP source and destination ports used for the reverse traffic before it can send packets to that host. Thus, if a host uses symmetric RTP or symmetric RTCP, an attacker need only see one RTP or RTCP packet in order to attack either endpoint.

The document notes that this attack is similar to that of other UDP-based protocols that use one UDP port pair, such as DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Using one port for both directions means one observed packet tells an attacker both port numbers to send to. The document says this is the same exposure other single-port UDP protocols have.

viz.caption: WHERE SYMMETRIC PORTS ARE REQUIRED OR HELPFUL

items.title: NAT without an ALG
items.text: Required. The translator needs symmetric UDP ports to establish bidirectional traffic.

items.title: Session Border Controller
items.text: Required. Even with a media relay, symmetric UDP ports are needed to traverse an address-dependent NAT.

items.title: Firewall filtering
items.text: Helpful. The firewall can keep a more restrictive dynamic per-call port filter list.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Helpful. One port per direction is easier to debug and troubleshoot.
